content.comment_body: Hello everyone, how can I capture I/O status (such as protocol or port information) from [product_name] [article_no] in a way similar to the method described here: [url]? I am using FaqFactory software, which allows flexible creation of data protocols over ethernet (serial via TCP/IP). Best regards, [user_name]
Hello, if your SCADA system supports a [version_no] communication driver over ethernet, there is a good chance it will work.
Thank you, but unfortunately, I do not have the necessary driver in Azeotech DaqFactory. Best regards, [user_name]

Hi, I reviewed that SCADA program and its features, and I think using OPC could be a solution. PC Acces provides an OPC server capable of connecting to a [version_no] PLC, and therefore to a [product_name] as well. Try searching this forum for PC Acces. You might also want to check your SCADA developer’s support page to ask if [version_no] communication is possible. Since others likely have similar questions, a solution might already exist. Regards,

Over the recent long weekend I managed to get it working. I spent time using an ethernet packet analyzer to discover communication similar to what is described in [url] by SNATAX. Communication to [product_name] at its IP address and port 10001 utilizes specific packets: for example, for status requests (Status?), mode (Mode?), stop/run commands and reading all statuses (which yields a 70-byte packet). Investigation of this data packet provides access to all inputs and outputs (e.g., byte 4 contains codes for I1-I8, byte 5 for I9-I16, etc.). I created a new protocol definition in Azeotech DaqFactory, allowing reliable visualization of necessary [product_name] data on my PC. This procedure depends heavily on the SCADA software you are using. Feel free to ask further questions. Regards, [user_name]

analysis.insight_summary: Users discussed the challenges and solutions for accessing and visualizing I/O status from a [company_name] [product_name] [article_no] using third-party SCADA software. Frequent issues include the absence of native driver support and limited protocol documentation, often necessitating protocol reverse-engineering and manual integration. The conversation shows that network traffic analysis and custom protocol configuration can enable successful integration, highlighting the need for better third-party support and clearer documentation.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect easy integration between [product_name] [article_no] and third-party SCADA software, preferably through standard protocols, detailed documentation, or existing drivers, to facilitate dependable and smooth visualization of I/O data.
